title: How to work satin stitch in cross-stitch
subtitle: Filling areas with parallel straight stitches for a smooth, flat surface
excerpt: Satin stitch is a filling stitch worked as parallel straight stitches laid side by side across an area. In cross-stitch it is used to fill small shapes such as flower centres, eyes, or monogram letters where a flat, solid texture is needed rather than the textured grid of cross-stitch. The stitches should lie smooth and even with no fabric showing between them.
sourceNotes: Satin stitch technique used as accent in cross-stitch work. Weldon's Practical Needlework series (1880s), Internet Archive. Standard guidance in major cross-stitch publisher guides.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads.
The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch.

content.text: Satin stitch fills a shape with straight, parallel
threads laid closely together so that no
shows between them. The result is smooth and has a slight sheen from the thread surface. It works best for small areas; large satin-stitch areas are prone to sagging and snagging.
Outline the area to be filled first with a running stitch or back stitch if the shape has a defined edge. The outline gives the satin stitch a clean boundary to work up to.

Bring the needle up at one edge of the shape. Take a straight stitch across to the opposite edge, exactly spanning the shape. Insert the needle just outside the outline if there is one, or just at the shape boundary if working without an outline.

Bring the needle up directly beside the first stitch. Keep each successive stitch parallel to the previous one, and close enough that no fabric shows between them. The threads should touch without overlapping.
Work at a consistent angle across the shape: vertical, horizontal, or diagonal at 45 degrees. Mixed angle stitches read as uneven fill. Check the angle regularly by holding the piece at arm's length.
End the thread by weaving under existing stitches on the back. Keep the back as neat as possible; a bulky back on a satin-stitch area creates visible lumps from the front.

items.symptom: Fabric shows between the satin stitches
items.cause: The stitches were placed too far apart, or the thread tension pulled them away from each other.
items.fix: Keep stitches closely spaced and pull each stitch snug before moving to the next. If gaps appear after the stitching is complete, add a second layer of satin stitch over the first at the same angle to fill the gaps.

items.symptom: The filled area has ridges or the stitches buckle
items.cause: The thread tension was inconsistent, or the stitches crossed the Aida at an angle that is fighting the fabric grain.
items.fix: Keep tension even on each stitch. For an oval or circular shape, work satin stitches at 45 degrees to the grain of the Aida rather than along the weave; this gives a smoother result. For rectangular shapes, follow the weave direction.

content.text: A small filled dot — a flower centre or an eye — is an easy first satin-stitch accent. The shape is small so the number of stitches is limited, and a small dot is forgiving if the stitches are not perfectly even. Larger shapes require more patience and consistent tension to look smooth.
